title: Animal Welfare and Humane Handling of Sheep and Goat

lessons.title: Why animal welfare matters
lessons.html:
Animals feel pain and fear

Sheep and goats feel pain, fear and stress. At the abattoir they are in a strange place, with strange smells and noises. Our job is to keep them calm and make sure they do not suffer. This is called animal welfare.

The law

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty to animals a crime. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its rules also require humane handling and slaughter at abattoirs. A worker who is cruel can be charged and lose their job.

Good welfare is good business

  • Calm animals are easier and safer to handle.
  • Stress before slaughter can make meat darker, tougher and spoil faster.
  • Rough handling causes bruises. Bruised meat must be trimmed off, so the farmer gets paid less.

The five freedoms

A simple way to think about welfare is that animals should be:

  1. Free from hunger and thirst: water must always be available in the lairage.
  2. Free from discomfort: shade, shelter and space.
  3. Free from pain, injury and disease: injured or sick animals get attention quickly.
  4. Free to express normal behaviour: for example, sheep stay in a group.
  5. Free from fear and distress: quiet, calm handling.

lessons.title: How sheep and goats behave and how to move them
lessons.html:
Understanding sheep

  • Sheep are flock animals. A sheep alone panics. Move them in groups.
  • Sheep follow a leader. If the first one moves, the rest follow.
  • Sheep have wide vision but a blind spot right behind them. Do not stand directly behind them.
  • They move away from people. Use their flight zone: step into it to make them move, step out to make them stop.
  • They prefer to move uphill, towards light and towards other sheep.

Understanding goats

  • Goats are more curious and independent than sheep. They may turn back or climb.
  • Goats do not flock as tightly. Give them time.
  • Billy goats with horns can be dangerous. Stay alert.

Moving animals calmly

  1. Work quietly. Do not shout or whistle loudly.
  2. Move slowly and in small groups.
  3. Use a flag, paddle or rattle to guide. Do not touch the animal with it hard.
  4. Remove things that stop animals: shadows, shiny water, hanging objects, people standing in front of the race.
  5. Do not overfill the race or crowd pen.

Never

  • Never lift or drag a sheep by its wool, or a goat by its horns, ears, legs or tail.
  • Never kick, hit or throw an animal.
  • Never use a sharp stick or twist the tail.
  • Never use an electric prodder on sheep or goats unless your plant's procedure allows it, and never on the face or sensitive parts.

To catch a sheep, hold it under the jaw and at the back of the body. Your trainer will show you safe ways to handle sheep and goats.

lessons.title: Welfare in the lairage and at stunning
lessons.html:
Arrival and lairage

  • Off-load sheep and goats as soon as possible after the truck arrives.
  • Check every animal. Report dead, injured, lame, very weak or sick animals at once to the supervisor and the meat inspector.
  • Injured animals that are suffering are dealt with as an emergency according to the plant procedure and the meat inspector's instructions.
  • Keep pens clean, dry and not overcrowded.
  • Provide clean water in every pen at all times.
  • Keep horned and hornless animals, rams and ewes, or groups from different farms apart where your plant requires it.
  • Do not keep animals in the lairage longer than the plant procedure allows without feed.

At stunning

Stunning makes the animal unconscious so that it feels no pain during bleeding. Only trained, authorised workers may stun.

  • Move animals into the restrainer one by one, calmly.
  • Stun quickly once the animal is restrained. Do not leave an animal waiting in the restrainer.
  • Check for signs of an effective stun: the animal collapses, has no rhythmic breathing and does not blink when the eye is touched.
  • If an animal shows signs of waking, stun again at once and tell the supervisor.
  • Bleed quickly after stunning, within the time the plant procedure sets.

Your duty

If you see cruelty or an animal suffering, report it to your supervisor or the meat inspector. Protecting animals is everyone's job.

Key points

  • Cruelty to animals is a crime under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  • Sheep are flock animals: move them in groups, quietly.
  • Never lift sheep by the wool or goats by the horns.
  • Water must always be available in the lairage.
  • Re-stun at once if an animal shows signs of waking.
  • Report injured animals and any cruelty you see.
